This note records an earlier design investigation. The retained implementation
and current reproduction guidance are in
[the final compressed rank/select design](../compressed-rank-select/index.qmd).
Intermediate implementations and their runners were removed during cleanup.

## Scope and conclusion

This study concerned the earlier `RankSelectSupportCompressed<4096,16>` and an
interpolation experiment that has since been removed. Source bits remain borrowed;
rank metadata uses one aligned 64-byte record per 16,384 source bits, with a
64-bit global prefix and 32 packed local prefixes. Both select directions are
studied. The implementation catalog now retains the final prefetch snapshot.

Superblock interpolation has little room on dense input: most sample intervals
span zero or one superblock. Basic-block population interpolation is accurate on dense input, but a
scalar-check-plus-SIMD-fallback screen did not establish an overall timing win.
A SIMD-group predictor for the wide secondary directory likewise did not
establish a consistent win at 2^30 or 2^34. The remaining hypothesis is starting
the source fetch earlier while rank metadata validates it. The
[retained design](../compressed-rank-select/index.qmd) uses this idea
with exact-position samples and metadata validation.
Prediction accuracy alone does not establish speed.

These are exploratory observations, not a promoted implementation. The
prediction-accuracy models below do not measure cache misses or hardware stage
latency.

## What the literature contributes

SPIDER predicts from two occurrence samples storing bit positions, then corrects
using rank data. Interleaved SPIDER's low-level samples are positions relative
to a superblock; non-interleaved SPIDER stores absolute positions. Thus its
prediction identifies a basic block, whereas Pixie's current primary samples
identify only superblocks [@Laws2024, sections 2.2--2.5].

SIP suggests reusing a slope, inexpensive arithmetic, and switching to a short
scan when progress is poor; TIP uses three points to fit nonuniform keys
[@VanSandt2019, sections 3--4]. For Pixie's narrow path, there are fewer than 16
superblocks, and often only one or two. An extra point and a more complicated
model are hard to justify before proving that a cheaper one-point guess helps.
Repeated rank values also mean this is interval localization, not exact-key
search.

## Why the current global interpolation pays extra

For one-based target rank `k`, the selected superblock satisfies

$$R(s) < k \le R(s) + P(s),$$

where `R(s)` is the prefix before the superblock and `P(s)` its population in the
requested direction. Both values are in one rank record: the global prefix at
the front and the terminal local prefix at the end.

The registered interpolation variant loads the next sample's global rank,
loads the first sample's global rank when needed, and then probes global
starting ranks until two adjacent boundaries remain. It never accepts a probe
by testing the end of that same record. The adjacent bracket can therefore
require additional probes after a good prediction. Loading an upper rank
boundary also costs a distinct record when the answer is in the lower block.

Three temporary screens tested paired-sample linear search, a first-block check
followed by one interpolation and exact correction, and a sample-ID guess with
exact correction. All retain the existing rank packing and secondary directory.
The focused screens did not establish a convincing general improvement.
In particular, always decoding a neighboring sample has a cost even when the
secondary directory or homogeneous shortcut resolves the query.

## Query geometry at 2^30

The diagnostic uses the current generators and shifted query pool, with
262,144 queries per direction per input and deterministic source/query seeds
matching the full comparison harness. Homogeneous and wide paths are classified
before applying the narrow-search models. All modeled localizations are checked
against the baseline's exact select answer.

Percentages below refer to queries, rather than unique sample intervals.

| Input/direction | Span 0 (%) | Span 1 (%) | Span 2--15 (%) | Wide (%) | Homogeneous (%) |
| :-------------- | ---------: | ---------: | -------------: | -------: | --------------: |
| 50%, select1    |     49.948 |     50.052 |          0.000 |    0.000 |           0.000 |
| 50%, select0    |     50.082 |     49.918 |          0.000 |    0.000 |           0.000 |
| 12.5%, select1  |      0.000 |      0.916 |         99.084 |    0.000 |           0.000 |
| Sparse, select1 |      0.000 |      0.000 |          0.000 |  100.000 |           0.000 |
| Mixed, select1  |     44.377 |      0.486 |          4.926 |   50.212 |           0.000 |
| Runs, either    |      0.000 |      0.000 |          0.000 |    0.000 |         100.000 |

At 12.5% density, narrow linear search examines 1.998 distinct rank records per
query, the current interpolation model 2.501, and the sample-ID prediction
1.498. The selected record is included in these counts. These are distinct
records touched by a modeled query, not hardware load counts or cache misses.
The reduced count alone did not establish a timing win.

The asymmetry of the generated Cartesian-tree input matters: in the same audit,
select1's current interpolation model examines 1.001 records versus 1.498 for
linear search; select0 examines 1.500 versus 1.001. A density-dependent choice
cannot be inferred from the population alone, and both directions must remain
in the objective.

## Predict a group in the wide secondary directory

The primary narrow interval contains fewer than 16 superblocks, but the wide
secondary directory can contain hundreds of occupied-block endpoints. Its
current `grouped_lower_bound` first binary-searches the ends of 32-element
groups, then runs SIMD lower-bound in the selected group. The following model
compares this with guessing an endpoint index

$$\hat i = \left\lfloor\frac{r m}{4096}\right\rfloor,$$

where `r = (k-1) mod 4096` and `m` is the entry's endpoint count. The divisor is
constant: this is a multiply and shift, without new boundary-rank loads or a
floating-point division. The guessed group is `floor(i_hat / 32)`.

Run SIMD lower-bound in that group first. If its answer is after lane zero,
the preceding lane is below the key, which proves the global lower-bound by
monotonicity; there is no need to read the previous group. A hit in lane zero
requires checking the previous group's last endpoint, unless this is group zero.
If the key is beyond the guessed group, search to its right; if the predecessor
is already at least the key, search to its left. Exact corrections remain
required for arbitrary populations.

The diagnostic uses 262,144 queries per direction, counts distinct logical
endpoint groups, and checks the result against exact endpoint lower-bound. It
includes the SIMD group itself and any predecessor or binary-correction groups.
Single-endpoint entries retain the existing shortcut without endpoint reads.

| Input/direction | Wide queries (%) | Mean endpoints per wide query | Predicted group correct (%) | Current groups examined | Predicted groups examined |
| :-------------- | ---------------: | ----------------------------: | --------------------------: | ----------------------: | ------------------------: |
| Sparse/select1  |          100.000 |                       257.034 |                      95.863 |                   3.384 |                     1.126 |
| Sparse0/select0 |          100.000 |                       256.575 |                      95.887 |                   3.378 |                     1.124 |
| Mixed/select1   |           50.212 |                        57.738 |                      56.909 |                   1.891 |                     1.497 |
| Mixed0/select0  |           50.212 |                        57.738 |                      56.909 |                   1.891 |                     1.497 |

These are logical groups, not physical cache lines or measured cache misses.
Entries are not individually cache-line aligned, so a full SIMD group can cross
two lines. Binary endpoint probes read only a scalar value. The temporary timing screen described below did not establish a consistent
query-time benefit. A retained candidate would still need registered benchmarks
and shared specification validation before promotion.

A construction-time quality flag is a possible refinement. For each endpoint
`e_i`, its valid keys run from `e_(i-1)+1` through `e_i`, with `e_(-1)=-1`.
Since the predictor is monotone, checking both extremes bounds its error for
all keys. If the maximum endpoint-index error is at most 32, the correct group
is within one group of the prediction. The flag could select this bounded
correction path and leave other entries on existing search. Each interval stores at most one endpoint per occupied superblock, so its
count is bounded by `ceil(SIZE_MAX / 16384)` independently of the sampling
frequency. That leaves high bits of the existing count field available beyond
the current contiguity marker. A quality flag would therefore need no larger
entry, although its dispatch and correction costs still require measurement.

In this model, 99.720% and 99.920% of sparse-direction queries use entries that
satisfy that error bound; only 36.522% do in the mixed minority direction.
These percentages are weighted by queries, not the number of directory entries.
This supports testing a cheap predictor with an exact fallback or build-time
quality gate, rather than paying for a more elaborate interpolation model.

## Basic-block prediction from the existing rank record

Let `t = k - R(s)`, `p = P(s)`, and `b` be the number of valid basic blocks.
For a full superblock, `b = 32`. An inexpensive guess is

$$\hat j = \left\lfloor\frac{(t-1)b}{p}\right\rfloor.$$

The guard `p > 0` follows from exact superblock localization. For arbitrary
partial superblocks and rounded estimates, clamp the guess to `[0,b-1]`.
Decode local prefix counts `C(j)` and `C(j+1)`. Accept exactly when

$$C(\hat j) < t \le C(\hat j+1).$$

Otherwise use the current packed-prefix search. This handles empty basic blocks,
clustering, and repeated prefixes without relying on prediction accuracy.
Any arithmetic approximation is safe only because the exact test and fallback
remain authoritative.

The following model uses exact integer population interpolation after exact
superblock localization. The sample alternatives interpolate physical positions
between two occurrence samples, using either exact bit positions or the centers
of their 512-bit quantization bins. All sample positions are obtained from exact
select, not a learned approximation. The final sample is a synthetic end-of-input
endpoint; its remaining occurrence count is used as the denominator.

| Input/direction | Existing-record guess correct basic block (%) | 512-bit samples, centered (%) | Exact-bit samples (%) |
| :-------------- | --------------------------------------------: | ----------------------------: | --------------------: |
| 12.5%, select1  |                                        79.542 |                        64.708 |                70.778 |
| 50%, select1    |                                        92.231 |                        77.470 |                94.459 |
| 50%, select0    |                                        92.184 |                        77.359 |                94.468 |
| 87.5%, select1  |                                        97.043 |                        78.305 |                98.410 |
| Sparse, select1 |                                        14.524 |                         1.007 |                 0.990 |
| Mixed, select1  |                                        83.653 |                        34.189 |                41.961 |
| FNBP, select1   |                                        99.461 |                        53.766 |                99.477 |

These percentages cover all modeled queries, including ones that existing
homogeneous or secondary-directory paths already handle. They quantify the
candidate predictions, not the net benefit of routing every query through them.
In particular, retain the homogeneous shortcut and the sparse secondary index.

Sparse populations are poorly predictable at basic-block granularity even after
exact superblock localization. A speculative scalar check should be bypassed
when confidence is low. The temporary screen gates it at population 512, an
exploratory threshold rather than an accepted policy; the audit's unconditional
accuracy figures above do not depend on that gate.

## More precise samples: space and limits

Re-encoding the exact sample positions with the existing blocked monotone
primitive gives the following model at 50% density and 2^30 source bits:

| Resolution | Two directions' sample storage (MiB) | Added source overhead vs superblock samples (percentage points) |
| :--------- | -----------------------------------: | ------------------------------------------------------------: |
| Superblock |                                0.188 |                                                         0.000 |
| 512 bits   |                                0.312 |                                                         0.098 |
| Exact bit  |                                0.625 |                                                         0.342 |

This compares the plain monotone sample containers, not the entire select index:
wide bitmaps, exception entries, and owning-index overhead are excluded. It is a
re-encoding model, not a production layout or a guarantee for every distribution.

Finer samples could predict the basic block before loading its rank record,
allowing a speculative source prefetch to overlap rank validation. That is a
hypothesis: a 77% accurate 512-bit prediction can fetch an unnecessary source line
on roughly 23% of these dense queries. Exact-bit samples improve accuracy to
about 94.5% but enlarge payloads and may add sample cache-line accesses.

The existing-record prediction is later in the dependency chain, but already
has about 92.2% accuracy here and needs no sample-space increase. It is the
smaller first experiment. If it helps, prefetching its predicted source block
while checking local prefixes is a separate experiment, with incorrect-prefetch
rates and actual cache counters measured independently.

## Experimental method and next decision

The temporary screens use the full-suite source generators, shifted 64-KiB query
pool, GCC 13.3 with `-O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native`, Ryzen 7 8845HS under WSL2,
serial processes pinned to CPU 0, both select directions, three independent
launches, and rotating operation/backend order. Query timing excludes source
construction, reference validation, and I/O. The first screen covers nine input
patterns at 2^30; the basic-block screen covers 50%, 12.5%, mixed, sparse, and
Cartesian-tree input. Each operation uses a 0.05-second warmup and 0.25-second
minimum. A paired-sample linear control isolates local prediction from the
existing experiment's global interpolation.

Temporary variants undergo reference validation on four shifted-pool passes
before each timed process, plus exhaustive select checks on structured short
and multi-superblock inputs, including invalid ranks, partial blocks, empty
gaps, and dirty padding. This does not replace the shared specification suite
or registered benchmark required before retaining or promoting a new library
implementation.

The local screen tested exact 32-bit integer division and a clamped float
estimate, two scalar prefix checks, and the existing SIMD fallback. Both keep
the paired-sample linear control's global localization. The screen did not
establish an overall win; per-operation variability was substantial. Production
code and the registered interpolation implementation remain unchanged.

A further temporary screen tested interpolation into SIMD groups of the wide
secondary directory, using an occurrence-proportional group guess, exact SIMD
checks, and bounded binary correction. It also tested direct search for a
single group and a minimum-group gate. Native and AVX2 sanitizer validation
covered approximately 26 million endpoint searches and 81 million select
queries, including duplicates, skew, partial groups, gaps, and dirty padding.
The screen covered five patterns at 2^30 and compared the unrestricted
predictor with the control on sparse, complemented sparse, and mixed inputs
at 2^34. Three independent launches per case did not establish a consistent
overall win; the larger runs had substantial variability. These temporary
kernels are not retained or promoted. Construction-time quality bounds remain
an untested hypothesis, rather than a demonstrated benefit.

A range-classification screen subsequently stored one medium-range bit per
sample, retaining the existing wide map. Spans of zero or one superblock used
production scanning, spans from two through fifteen used interpolation, and
larger spans retained the secondary directory. Only medium queries decoded a
neighboring sample. It tested the original interpolation loop, a first-block
check with exact correction, and an outlined version that kept medium dispatch
inside the narrow path. The nine standard patterns at 2^30 showed no consistent
overall benefit. Additional random 6.25%, 3.125%, and 1.5625% populations covered
longer medium intervals and the wide boundary; the outlined implementation also
failed to establish an advantage there.

Native and AVX2 AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer differential checks
covered all three classes, sample-group boundaries, repeated rank prefixes,
gaps, partial words, and sample frequencies 8, 4096, and 65536. Query-only perf
runs used equal fixed select counts and non-multiplexed event groups. On the
population with roughly eight-superblock intervals, interpolation reduced
reported L1 load misses but increased instructions and cycles. The code reads
boundary ranks before calculating a probe, introducing a dependency chain that
sequential scanning can avoid. That is a plausible explanation for the measured
loss, rather than evidence that the class bitmap or fewer cache misses alone
makes the operation faster. These temporary variants are not promoted.

A separate remaining experiment is memory overlap: predict a source block,
start its fetch, then validate with the existing rank search. Compare prediction from the
loaded rank record against prediction from more precise samples. Measure extra
source fetches when the guess is wrong and sample-payload cache-line costs, as
well as balanced rank-plus-select query time and allocated space. Keep the
homogeneous shortcut and wide secondary directory. An early prefetch is not an
answer; exact rank checks must still choose the block.

Keep repeated interpolation and three-point models secondary until a workload
actually presents enough unresolved rank records for them to save. The current
experiments justify investigating latency overlap, not promoting a more
complicated search or assuming a cache-miss reduction.
